title: UNIT 4: POLYMERS
notes:
✓ Polymers → Large molecules made up of many interconnected repeating units. They are important materials found in both living organisms and manufactured products.
Natural polymers include cellulose, starch, proteins, natural rubber, and nucleic acids, while synthetic polymers include polyethylene, polypropylene, PVC, nylon, polyester, and many other plastics.

✓ Polymer structure → May be linear, slightly branched, or highly interconnected. The structure determines many of their physical and chemical properties and therefore determines their applications.

title: 4.1 Polymer and Monomer
notes:
✓ Polymer → A large chain-like molecule formed from many smaller molecules called monomers. A polymer may contain a very large number of monomer units. Molecules containing fewer repeating units are commonly called oligomers.

✓ Polymer → Comes from the Greek words poly, meaning "many," and meros, meaning "part."

✓ Polymer structure → Polymers may be linear, slightly branched, or highly interconnected. Highly interconnected polymers can form large three-dimensional networks.

✓ Monomer → A small molecule that acts as a basic building block for a polymer. Monomers combine through chemical reactions called polymerization reactions.

◆ EXAMPLES
Ethene → Polyethylene
Glucose → Cellulose
Amino acids → Proteins

✓ Degree of polymerization (DP) → The number of repeating units in a polymer. The relative molar mass of a polymer can be related to the relative molar mass of its repeating unit and the degree of polymerization.

title: 4.1.1 Repeating Units and Degree of Polymerization
notes:
✓ Repeating unit → The structural part that occurs repeatedly along a polymer chain.
In many addition polymers, the repeating unit can be obtained from the monomer by opening the multiple bond and forming bonds with neighboring units.

◆ EXAMPLE
Ethene:
CH₂=CH₂

Polyethylene:
[–CH₂–CH₂–]ₙ

✓ Repeating unit → –CH₂–CH₂–
✓ n → Represents the number of repeating units in the polymer and is related to the degree of polymerization (DP).

✓ Approximate relative molar mass of polymer = Relative molar mass of repeating unit × Degree of polymerization.

→ Increasing the number of repeating units generally produces a polymer with a larger molecular mass.

title: 4.2 Polymerization Reactions
notes:
✓ Polymerization → The chemical change by which monomer molecules combine to form a polymer.

✓ Monomer functionality → Monomers with two reactive functional groups can form mainly linear chain-like polymers, while monomers with higher functionality can form branched or cross-linked network structures.

◆ TWO MAJOR TYPES
◆ Addition polymerization
◆ Condensation polymerization

→ The type of polymerization depends mainly on the structure and functional groups of the monomers involved.

title: 4.2.1 Addition Polymerization
notes:
✓ Addition polymerization → A chain-growth polymerization in which monomer molecules are added one at a time to a growing polymer chain. It normally involves unsaturated monomers containing carbon-carbon double or triple bonds.

✓ Alkene polymerization → The carbon-carbon double bond is converted into a single bond as the monomer becomes part of the polymer chain.

◆ EXAMPLE: POLYETHYLENE
nCH₂=CH₂ → [–CH₂–CH₂–]ₙ
Ethene → Polyethylene

◆ EXAMPLE: POLYSTYRENE
nCH₂=CH–C₆H₅ → [–CH₂–CH(C₆H₅)–]ₙ

✓ Addition polymerization → No small molecule such as water is normally eliminated. The atoms of the monomer become part of the polymer chain.

◆ IMPORTANT ADDITION POLYMERS
Polyethylene, polypropylene, PVC, PMMA, Teflon, polystyrene, and natural rubber.

title: 4.2.2 Steps of Addition Polymerization
notes:
✓ Addition polymerization → Takes place through three main steps in chain-growth polymerization.

◆ 1. CHAIN INITIATION
The polymerization begins when a reactive initiator produces an active center. The initiator may produce a free radical, cation, or anion. This active species attacks the multiple bond of a monomer and starts the growing chain.

◆ 2. CHAIN PROPAGATION
Additional monomer molecules add successively to the active end of the growing polymer chain. The active center remains at the end of the growing chain, allowing the chain to continue increasing in length.

◆ 3. CHAIN TERMINATION
The chain reaction eventually stops when the active center is neutralized or otherwise destroyed. The resulting polymer chain is no longer able to continue propagating.

✓ Free-radical polymerization → An important form of addition polymerization.
Cationic and anionic polymerization are other possible chain-growth mechanisms.

title: 4.2.3 Finding a Monomer from a Polymer
notes:
✓ Monomer identification → For many addition polymers, the monomer can be identified by examining the repeating unit and restoring the multiple bond that was present in the original monomer.

◆ POLYETHYLENE
[–CH₂–CH₂–]ₙ
Restore the double bond:
CH₂=CH₂
→ Monomer = Ethene.

◆ PVC
[–CH₂–CHCl–]ₙ
Restore the double bond:
CH₂=CHCl
→ Monomer = Vinyl chloride (chloroethene).

✓ Molecular formula relationship → The molecular formula of an addition polymer is related to n times the formula of its monomer because the monomer units join together without eliminating small molecules.

✓ Number of monomer units:
n = Molar mass of polymer ÷ Molar mass of monomer.

title: 4.2.4 Condensation Polymerization
notes:
✓ Condensation polymerization → A polymerization process in which monomer molecules combine while a small molecule, commonly water or methanol, is eliminated as a by-product.

✓ Condensation polymerization → Also called step-growth polymerization. The monomers generally contain two or more functional groups that can react with one another.

◆ TYPICAL REACTIONS
Dibasic acids + diamines → Polyamides
Dibasic acids + diols → Polyesters

✓ Simplified polyester formation:
Diol + Dicarboxylic acid → Polyester + water

✓ Condensation polymers → May be natural or synthetic.
Natural examples include proteins, starch, and cellulose. Synthetic examples include Nylon 66, Dacron/polyethylene terephthalate, and Bakelite.

title: 4.2.5 Nylon 66
notes:
✓ Nylon 66 → A synthetic polyamide and a condensation polymer. It is a copolymer made from two different monomers: hexamethylene diamine and adipic acid.

◆ MONOMERS
Hexamethylene diamine:
H₂N–(CH₂)₆–NH₂

Adipic acid:
HOOC–(CH₂)₄–COOH

✓ Polymerization → Amide bonds form and water is eliminated.

✓ Nylon 66 → Has good strength and is useful for producing fibers and other durable materials.

◆ IMPORTANT USES
Parachutes
Ropes
Clothes
Stockings
Hair combs
Rugs and carpets
Reinforcement of automobile tires

✓ Number 66 → Refers to the six carbon atoms present in each of the two monomers used to produce Nylon 66.

title: 4.2.6 Polyester and Dacron
notes:
✓ Dacron → A polyester and an important condensation polymer. It is also known as polyethylene terephthalate (PET/PTE).

◆ RAW MATERIALS
Terephthalic acid
Ethylene glycol (1,2-ethanediol)

✓ Polymerization → Forms ester linkages and eliminates water.

✓ Dacron properties → Strength, impact resistance, transparency, and durability.

◆ USES
Synthetic fibers
Durable fabrics when blended with cotton
Bottles
Packaging materials

✓ General polyester formation:
Diol + Dicarboxylic acid → Polyester + H₂O

✓ Functional groups involved → Hydroxyl (–OH) and carboxyl (–COOH) groups.

title: 4.2.7 Bakelite
notes:
✓ Bakelite → A synthetic thermosetting polymer produced from phenol and formaldehyde. It is a condensation polymer.

✓ Structure → Bakelite forms a highly cross-linked structure. Because of this structure, it is hard, rigid, and resistant to heat and mechanical stress.

✓ Heating behavior → Unlike thermoplastics, Bakelite does not soften and flow when heated. Strong heating eventually causes irreversible decomposition rather than allowing the material to be remolded.

◆ USES
Electrical components
Switches
Handles
Other products requiring heat resistance, rigidity, and electrical insulation.

title: 4.3 Classification of Polymers
notes:
✓ Polymers can be classified according to several criteria.

◆ CLASSIFICATION CRITERIA
Types of monomers used
Nature of the polymerization reaction
Natural or synthetic origin
Response to heat

✓ Based on monomers → Homopolymers or copolymers.
✓ Based on polymerization reaction → Addition polymers or condensation polymers.
✓ Based on origin → Natural polymers or synthetic polymers.
✓ Based on response to heat → Thermoplastics or thermosetting polymers.

title: 4.3.1 Homopolymers
notes:
✓ Homopolymer → A polymer prepared from only one type of monomer.

◆ EXAMPLE
Polyethylene is a homopolymer because it is produced from only one type of monomer, ethene.

nCH₂=CH₂ → [–CH₂–CH₂–]ₙ
Ethene → Polyethylene

→ The repeating units in a homopolymer are derived from the same monomer type.

✓ Copolymer → A polymer containing more than one kind of monomer.

title: 4.3.2 Copolymers
notes:
✓ Copolymer → A polymer prepared from more than one kind of monomer unit.

◆ EXAMPLE
Ethene + propene → Copolymer containing two different repeating units.

✓ Copolymer arrangement → Different monomer units can be arranged in different ways along the chain.

◆ RANDOM COPOLYMER
Different monomer units are arranged in no regular sequence.
Example pattern:
A–B–B–A–A–A–B–A–A

◆ REGULAR COPOLYMER
Different monomer units follow a regular sequence, such as alternating units.
Example pattern:
A–B–A–B–A–B–A–B

→ Using different monomers allows the properties of a polymer to be modified, such as melting point, density, strength, and flexibility.

title: 4.3.3 Natural Polymers
notes:
✓ Natural polymers → Polymers that occur naturally and can be extracted from living organisms or natural materials. They are often called biopolymers.

◆ IMPORTANT GROUPS
Carbohydrates
Proteins
Natural fibers
Natural rubber
Nucleic acids

◆ EXAMPLES
Starch, cellulose, gums, enzymes, wool, silk, cotton, natural rubber, RNA, and DNA.

✓ Functions → Natural polymers provide structural materials, store or supply energy, participate in physiological processes, and carry genetic information.

→ Wood and cotton contain cellulose. Hair, skin, and muscles contain proteins. Natural rubber contains polyisoprene.

title: 4.3.4 Carbohydrates as Natural Polymers
notes:
✓ Carbohydrates → An important group of natural compounds. The unit discusses monosaccharides, disaccharides, and polysaccharides.

◆ MONOSACCHARIDES
Simple sugars that act as basic units for larger carbohydrates.
Examples: glucose, fructose, galactose, and ribose.

◆ DISACCHARIDES
Contain two monosaccharide units joined together.
Examples: sucrose, lactose, and maltose.

◆ POLYSACCHARIDES
Large carbohydrate molecules containing many sugar units.
Examples: starch, cellulose, and gums.

✓ Starch → An important plant storage polysaccharide.
✓ Cellulose → A major structural material in plant cell walls.

→ Although starch and cellulose are both composed of glucose-derived units, differences in their structures and linkages give them different properties and biological functions.

title: 4.3.5 Starch and Cellulose
notes:
✓ Starch and cellulose → Natural polysaccharides made from glucose units, but their structures and functions are different.

◆ STARCH
Starch is a storage material in plants. It is composed of many glucose units joined together and is found in foods such as grains and other plant materials.

◆ CELLULOSE
Cellulose is a structural polysaccharide. It is an important component of plant cell walls and is found in materials such as wood and cotton.

→ Both are natural polymers, but the arrangement and bonding of their glucose units are different. These structural differences produce very different properties.

✓ Cellulose → Gives plants strength and structural support.
✓ Starch → Mainly serves as an energy-storage material.

title: 4.3.6 Proteins and Nucleic Acids
notes:
✓ Proteins → Natural polymers formed from amino acid units. Amino acids contain functional groups that allow them to join together to form long chains.

◆ PROTEIN FUNCTIONS
Structural support
Catalysis
Transport
Regulation of biological processes

✓ Nucleic acids → Natural polymers. DNA and RNA are examples.
✓ DNA → Stores genetic information.
✓ RNA → Participates in the expression and transfer of genetic information.

→ Proteins and nucleic acids demonstrate that polymers are not limited to synthetic plastics. Many essential substances in living organisms are polymeric materials.

title: 4.3.7 Natural Rubber
notes:
✓ Natural rubber → A natural polymer made mainly from polyisoprene. Its monomer is isoprene.

✓ Elasticity → Natural rubber can stretch and return toward its original shape, making it useful where flexibility and elasticity are required.

◆ USES
Rubber materials
Elastic components
Other applications where flexibility is useful

✓ Vulcanization → A chemical treatment that introduces cross-links between polymer chains and produces a stronger and more durable material.

→ Vulcanized rubber is classified among thermosetting materials in the textbook's classification.

title: 4.3.8 Synthetic Polymers
notes:
✓ Synthetic polymers → Human-made polymers produced through chemical processes. They are sometimes broadly referred to as plastics, although not every polymeric material is necessarily a conventional plastic.

✓ Useful properties → Synthetic polymers may be lightweight, strong, flexible, chemically resistant, electrically insulating, transparent, or heat resistant.

◆ IMPORTANT SYNTHETIC POLYMERS
Polyethylene
Polypropylene
Polyvinyl chloride (PVC)
Polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA)
Polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE/Teflon)
Polystyrene
Nylon
Polyester/Dacron
Bakelite

title: 4.3.9 Polyethylene
notes:
✓ Polyethylene → Produced by addition polymerization of ethene.

Monomer:
CH₂=CH₂

Polymer:
[–CH₂–CH₂–]ₙ

✓ Properties → No taste or odor, lightweight, relatively inexpensive, and useful for many everyday products.

◆ USES
Squeeze bottles
Plastic wrapping
Garment bags
Trash bags
Electrical insulation
Tubes and containers

✓ Classification → Polyethylene is a thermoplastic because it can soften when heated and can be remolded or reprocessed.

title: 4.3.10 Polypropylene
notes:
✓ Polypropylene → Produced by addition polymerization of propene (propylene).

Monomer:
CH₂=CH–CH₃

Polymer:
[–CH₂–CH(CH₃)–]ₙ

✓ Properties → Stronger than polyethylene and has useful resistance to many chemicals and everyday conditions.

◆ USES
Food containers
Ropes
Fishing nets
Carpets
Bottles
Household products

→ Its useful strength and relatively low mass make it an important synthetic polymer.

title: 4.3.11 Polyvinyl Chloride (PVC)
notes:
✓ Polyvinyl chloride (PVC) → Produced by polymerization of vinyl chloride (chloroethene).

Monomer:
CH₂=CHCl

Polymer:
[–CH₂–CHCl–]ₙ

✓ PVC → An important synthetic plastic widely used because of its durability and useful physical properties.

◆ MAJOR APPLICATIONS
Pipes
Leather-like materials
Shoes
Raincoats
Aprons
Wallpaper
Floor tiles
Phonograph records

→ PVC can be made in different forms depending on its formulation and processing.

title: 4.3.12 Polymethyl Methacrylate (PMMA)
notes:
✓ Polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA) → Also known by trade names such as Perspex, Lucite, or Plexiglass.

✓ Monomer:
CH₂=C(CH₃)COOCH₃

✓ Properties → Lightweight and glass-like. Its transparency makes it useful as a substitute for glass in some applications.

◆ APPLICATIONS
Airplane windows
Streetlights
Transparent sheets
Other applications requiring a lightweight glass-like material

✓ Classification → PMMA is an addition polymer because its monomer contains a carbon-carbon double bond.

title: 4.3.13 Polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE/Teflon)
notes:
✓ Polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) → Commonly known as Teflon. It is produced by addition polymerization of tetrafluoroethylene.

Monomer:
CF₂=CF₂

✓ Properties → Excellent resistance to chemical attack and useful properties over a wide temperature range. The textbook notes a working range of approximately –73°C to 260°C.

✓ Coefficient of friction → PTFE has a very low coefficient of friction, giving it a slippery or waxy surface.

◆ USES
Coating cooking utensils
Non-stick surfaces
Electrical insulation
Teflon tape
Applications requiring chemical resistance and low friction

→ The low friction and non-stick properties make PTFE particularly useful in food preparation equipment.

title: 4.3.14 Polystyrene
notes:
✓ Polystyrene → An addition polymer produced from styrene.

Monomer:
CH₂=CH–C₆H₅

Polymer:
[–CH₂–CH(C₆H₅)–]ₙ

✓ Properties → Its properties depend on its form and processing. It can be produced as a rigid plastic or as an expanded foam.

✓ Applications → Packaging and other products where lightweight and easily shaped polymer materials are useful.

title: 4.3.15 Thermoplastic Polymers
notes:
✓ Thermoplastic polymers → Polymers that melt or soften when heated and become solid again when cooled. They are generally made of essentially linear or lightly branched polymer molecules.

✓ Reshaping → Thermoplastics can generally be softened and reshaped repeatedly. They can generally be remelted and reprocessed, making many thermoplastics suitable for recycling.

◆ EXAMPLES
Polyethylene
Polypropylene
Polyvinyl chloride
Teflon
PMMA
Nylon
Polyester/Dacron
Polystyrene
Polyamides

→ The ability to soften on heating is an important difference between thermoplastics and thermosetting polymers.

title: 4.3.16 Thermosetting Polymers
notes:
✓ Thermosetting polymers → Polymers that do not melt when heated. At sufficiently high temperatures they undergo irreversible decomposition instead.

✓ Structure → Thermosetting polymers contain substantial cross-linking and form extensive three-dimensional networks of covalent bonds.

→ Their cross-linked structure gives them resistance to heat, corrosion, and mechanical stress.

◆ EXAMPLES
Bakelite
Epoxy resin
Cyanate esters
Fiber-glass reinforced thermosets
Polyester resins
Polyurethane
Silicone resins
Vinyl esters
Vulcanized rubber

✓ Once permanently cured → A thermosetting polymer cannot be softened and remolded by heating like a thermoplastic.

title: 4.3.17 Thermoplastics vs Thermosetting Polymers
notes:
◆ THERMOPLASTICS
✓ Soften or melt when heated.
✓ Solidify when cooled.
✓ Can generally be reheated and reshaped.
✓ Usually have linear or lightly branched structures.
✓ Can generally be remelted and reprocessed.
✓ Examples → Polyethylene, polypropylene, PVC, PMMA, Teflon, nylon, polyester, and polystyrene.

◆ THERMOSETTING POLYMERS
✓ Do not melt when reheated after curing.
✓ Decompose at sufficiently high temperatures.
✓ Have extensive three-dimensional cross-linking.
✓ Are generally resistant to heat and mechanical stress.
✓ Cannot normally be remolded by heating.
✓ Examples → Bakelite, epoxy resin, and vulcanized rubber.

◆ KEY DIFFERENCE
Thermoplastic → Can soften and be reshaped by heating.
Thermosetting → Permanently cross-linked and cannot be remolded by heating.

title: 4.3.18 Classification by Polymerization Reaction
notes:
✓ Polymers can also be classified according to the chemical reaction used to produce them.

◆ ADDITION POLYMERS
Formed by addition reactions of unsaturated monomers. The multiple bond of the monomer participates in forming the polymer chain.

✓ Examples → Polyethylene, polypropylene, PVC, PMMA, Teflon, polystyrene, and natural rubber.

◆ CONDENSATION POLYMERS
Formed from monomers in reactions accompanied by the loss of a small molecule, usually water.

✓ Examples → Nylon, polyester, Bakelite, proteins, starch, and cellulose.

→ The presence or absence of a small-molecule by-product is an important distinction between the two types.

title: 4.3.19 Structure, Properties and Uses
notes:
✓ Polymer properties → Depend on molecular structure. Factors such as the type of monomer, chain arrangement, branching, cross-linking, functional groups, and intermolecular interactions affect the behavior of a polymer.

◆ EXAMPLES
Polyethylene → Lightweight and useful for bags, bottles, wrapping, and insulation.
Polypropylene → Stronger than polyethylene and useful for ropes, fishing nets, carpets, containers, and bottles.
PVC → Durable and useful for pipes, flooring, raincoats, and other products.
PMMA → Transparent and lightweight, making it useful as a glass substitute.
PTFE → Chemically resistant and has very low friction, making it useful for non-stick coatings and electrical insulation.

→ The structure of a polymer determines its properties, and its properties determine suitable applications.

title: UNIT 4 — MUST REMEMBER
notes:
✓ POLYMER → A large molecule built from many interconnected repeating units.
✓ MONOMER → A small molecule used as a basic building block for a polymer.
✓ HOMOPOLYMER → Polymer made from one type of monomer.
✓ COPOLYMER → Polymer made from more than one type of monomer.
✓ RANDOM COPOLYMER → Different monomer units arranged randomly.
✓ REGULAR COPOLYMER → Different monomer units arranged in a regular sequence.
✓ ADDITION POLYMERIZATION → Chain-growth polymerization involving unsaturated monomers; no small molecule is normally eliminated.
✓ CONDENSATION POLYMERIZATION → Polymerization in which monomers combine with elimination of a small molecule, commonly water.

◆ NATURAL POLYMERS
Starch, cellulose, proteins, natural rubber, RNA, DNA, wool, silk, and cotton.

◆ SYNTHETIC POLYMERS
Polyethylene, polypropylene, PVC, PMMA, Teflon, polystyrene, nylon, polyester, and Bakelite.

✓ THERMOPLASTIC → Softens or melts on heating and can generally be reshaped.
✓ THERMOSETTING → Highly cross-linked polymer that does not melt on reheating and eventually decomposes.

◆ IMPORTANT MONOMER → POLYMER PAIRS
Ethene → Polyethylene
Propene → Polypropylene
Vinyl chloride → PVC
Methyl methacrylate → PMMA
Tetrafluoroethylene → PTFE/Teflon
Styrene → Polystyrene
Isoprene → Natural rubber
Hexamethylene diamine + adipic acid → Nylon 66
Ethylene glycol + terephthalic acid → Dacron/PET
Phenol + formaldehyde → Bakelite

◆ IMPORTANT ADDITION REACTION
nCH₂=CH₂ → [–CH₂–CH₂–]ₙ

✓ IMPORTANT IDEA
The properties and applications of polymers depend strongly on their molecular structures. Thermoplastics can be reshaped by heating, whereas thermosetting polymers are permanently cross-linked and cannot be remolded by heating.
